commitNotes.9fb87008a:
nvidia_write_aq_drm() pinned Aquamarine's AQ_DRM_DEVICES to the NVIDIA
card alone whenever a hybrid GPU setup was detected. On most hybrid
laptops the internal panel is wired to the iGPU, not the dGPU, so this
handed Hyprland a render device with no connector for the built-in
screen — session never comes up, looks like a boot failure.

Confirmed on an HP Omen Max 16 (RTX 5080): env.lua carried
  hl.env("AQ_DRM_DEVICES", "/dev/dri/by-path/pci-0000:02:00.0-card")
with no iGPU entry, matching this exact failure mode.

A joined-list fix (NVIDIA first, plus every other connector-capable
card, so the panel's actual owning GPU stayed reachable) was tried
before committing anything, on the theory that the missing connector
was the root cause. Testing on the same hardware showed it still
failed to boot. That points to the actual problem being NVIDIA's side
of the multi-GPU render/blit handoff itself, not connector coverage —
a known-fragile path per the Hyprland wiki's own multi-GPU/NVIDIA
note
commitNotes.84127def8:
The initramfs was told i915 for every Intel card. Which of i915 and xe claims a
part is the kernel's call and it moves from one release to the next, so on the
newest hardware — where xe takes it — the initramfs carried a module that was
not driving anything and early KMS quietly did not happen. Nothing broke; the
driver still loaded later, and the flicker-free boot it was there for simply
got missing on the parts most likely to want it.

Reading it off the card settles it. The generation tiers were no help: the one
covering Xe spans parts on both sides of the split, so mapping tier to module
would have put xe in front of an Arrow Lake, which is worse than the hardcoded
answer it replaced. Asking what is bound cannot disagree with the kernel, and
follows it for free the release a default changes. i915 when nothing answers,
which is both the older parts' module and what was named here before.

The card list the compositor is given grew a seam for its lookup directory at
the same time, b
commitNotes.cd61965e7:
The box takes a string, but a caller with a color rather than a typed one hands
over whatever Qt makes of it — and Qt writes a color that carries alpha as nine
digits, the leading pair being that alpha. Nothing here expected them. The
swatch painted the alpha too, so a color the interface draws at a tenth opacity
arrived as a near-invisible smear of itself; the box was sized for seven
characters and showed a fragment of the nine; and the reader that guards typing
rejects eight digits outright, so the value could not be edited back into shape
either. A color nobody could see, read, or correct.

The reader now takes that form and drops the alpha, and the swatch and the box
read through it rather than off the raw value. What a color is worth and how
much of it shows through are two settings here, and only the first belongs in a
box that says which color it is.
commitNotes.617184c4e:
The popup was taught to open under the widget that asked for it, but only along
one axis: the placement returned early on a vertical bar and the margin was
fixed at half the screen, so wherever the media widget sat on a side bar the
controls appeared at the middle. The widget there never published itself either,
so there was nothing to place against had the placement run.

It now measures the same way on either edge and slides along whichever axis the
bar leaves free — across under a top or bottom bar, up and down beside a left or
right one — clamped to the screen with the same gap at both ends. The stock
middle spot remains what is used until the widget has been measured, and
whenever it cannot be.
commitNotes.fd401b47e:
A field could be given a color but never returned to not having one: an emptied
box normalises to nothing, and nothing was read as a typo and refused. Clearing
it now says "no color of my own" wherever that is a state worth having.

Off unless asked for. A gradient lane cannot draw an empty string, so refusing
it there is still the right answer, and every field that exists today keeps the
behavior it had. It also takes a genuinely blank box rather than merely an
unparseable one, so a half-typed code still snaps back instead of quietly
dropping the color that was set.
commitNotes.cf85bd8bb:
The swatch took its height from the text control's drawn outline and the button
beside them took its own, so a row meant to be read as one control was three
things of two heights. Both now take the button's, which is the tallest of them
and the one with a hard edge to line up against.

The same component draws the border gradient colors, so those rows sit level too.

releases.summary: Works with newer LocalSend devices that now expect extra security during transfer
changes: Enable sending files to receivers that now require a certificate to connect
commits: 38d58c79a localsend: offer a certificate when a receiver asks for one

commitNotes.38d58c79a:
Receivers began requiring the sender to present a certificate during the TLS
handshake. Sending never offered one, so the connection was refused before a
byte of the file moved, and the failure arrived as a certificate alert rather
than as anything about the transfer. Nothing here changed; the other end did,
which is why this worked for months and then stopped.

One is generated on first use and kept, so a peer goes on seeing the same
device rather than a new one per transfer. Which certificate it is does not
matter to the handshake — that one is offered at all does. It is presented to
every receiver, since one that does not ask simply ignores it, and a receiver
that refuses to load it is no worse off than before.

commitNotes.47a6af33c:
A layout group is not always {widgets: [...]}. It can be a bare string, or
carry items instead, and the bar, its editor and the seeding pass all go
through one tolerant reader for exactly that reason. The scrub did not: it
read .widgets directly, saw nothing in a group written either other way, and
concluded the group was empty. Empty groups are dropped. So a config holding
one spacer anywhere and one older-form group anywhere lost the second on load
and had the loss written back, with no backup to undo it.

This is the same shape as the fault the widget seeding pass carried, which was
fixed by handing it the tolerant reader. The scrub gets the same treatment,
and one more guard besides: a group with nothing retired in it is now returned
exactly as it was read, in whatever form it was written. Only a group that
actually held a retired id is rewritten, which is the only case where changing
its form is the point.

While here, the spacer pivot no longer insists the spacer be alone in its
commitNotes.a22771894:
Every theme saved before the dock could move names no edge, and applying one
replaces config.json wholesale, so the key simply vanishes from the file. That
is the worst of both answers: the adapter keeps the value it already has, so the
dock stays put and nothing looks wrong, while the file on disk no longer says
where it goes. The next start reads no edge and falls back to the default, and
the dock moves somewhere the user never chose, one boot removed from the theme
switch that caused it.

The live edge is written in instead, so the screen and the file agree. A theme
that does name an edge still wins outright — that is the theme owning its
layout, which is the point — and this only fills the silence.
commitNotes.350ad10da:
The ripple lives inside the button's background, which the control insets on
both axes, but only the vertical inset was being taken off the press
coordinates — and the reach was measured across the whole control rather than
the background. Nothing showed it until dock buttons gained a left and right
inset, which put the ripple ten pixels off the pointer on a side dock.
commitNotes.ba1ba669b:
The dock was hardwired to the bottom, so a bottom bar and the dock
stacked on one edge and fought over the same hover strip. The dock
now takes a position - bottom, top, left or right - from a dropdown
that offers all four, renders vertically on the sides, and gives way
to the bar when the bar is moved onto the edge it saved. Asking for
the bar's own edge from the dock's setting is the one case the dock
does not give way: the bar crosses to the far side of its axis and
the dock takes what was asked for, because refusing the choice or
quietly answering with a different edge are both worse than moving
the thing that was not being talked about. One edge value drives the window anchors, the reveal
slide, the layout flow, the magnify origin, the running-window dots
and every popup's direction; the anchor sets swap through states
because a live flip through conditional bindings passes an illegal
three-anchor moment that wedges the layout. The bar and dock edges
resolve in one shared place th
commitNotes.f116b6620:
The built-in was hidden whenever any per-window bridge of the same
browser make existed, so with a second browser running unbridged its
only player vanished from the popup while the bar kept its title. No
name-level linkage ties a bridge to its browser - the bridge embeds
its own host pid while the browser names its player after its D-Bus
connection or its pid depending on version - but the bridge host is
always a child of the browser that owns the built-in's connection, so
a helper resolves both connections to processes and matches ancestry.
commitNotes.306812069:
The IPC handlers wrote the loader's active property directly, and an
imperative write severs its binding to the shared open flag - after
one IPC call the widget click, Esc, the global shortcut and the
transfer auto-close all stopped reaching the popup. Nothing consumes
the loader directly: the keybind already goes through the shared
flag, and the bridge extension never talks to the shell.
commitNotes.6593fdc24:
The editor offers a bar-managed widget back when a layout arrives
without one, floats such entries to the front of their group so drags
cannot reorder around something it does not show, and reads groups
through the shared ObjectUtils helper instead of a diverged copy.
Chromeless detection ignores entries the bar cannot render, a missing
enabled key counts as enabled everywhere, the space-taking widget
list lives in one predicate, media stops yielding when the window
title already stretches the pill, pilled groups no longer build a
hidden duplicate of every widget, and the timer tray can no longer be
squashed while its reveal animates.
commitNotes.a7cf2e745:
The side sections span the whole window, but on the floating style
the bar's visible body is inset by the gap, so their pills ran wider
than the bar they sat on while the center pills came out at the
bar's own width. Both side columns now inset by the same gap, and
every pill reads as one shape.
commitNotes.67f4fd306:
The meters beyond memory hid whenever anything was playing, wherever
the widget sat - the collapse exists to hand the shared pill's room
to media, and a resources widget in its own pill was shrinking for a
player it was not even next to. Standing alone it now keeps the full
readout; beside media it still hands the room back while a track
plays.
commitNotes.45c4db442:
With each side row carrying its own stretch filler, the left cluster
packs left and the right cluster packs right on their own, and the
spacer was a movable way of asking for what is now the fixed rule.
The widget is gone from the bar, the default layout and the customize
menu.

A layout saved before this still names the spacer, and the bar draws
nothing for an id it no longer knows — so the room the spacer held
disappears and every widget beside it slides over, on a bar the user
never asked to rearrange. Leaving that to the editor was not enough:
it only rewrites a section once someone opens it, so the bar stays
rearranged until they do. The config drops retired ids as it loads
instead, once, taking a group left holding nothing with them. The
editor reads the same list, so the two cannot come to disagree, and a
fresh install names no retired id and so is never written to at
startup — the one thing this file must not do while a first login is
seeding it from outside.

Dropping the widg
commitNotes.6b245fd1e:
The volume and media popups clamp their position to the screen, but
the shared hover popup placed itself purely by centring on its widget,
so weather, resources or the update indicator near a screen edge
pushed their popups past it. The same clamp now applies to every
popup that centers on a bar widget, on both bar orientations.
commitNotes.98515b5ca:
Fill meant two different things: share-the-set-width inside a center
pill, and take-the-section outside it. Splitting those claims, only
the widgets whose job is genuinely width still take a section — the
spacer, which exists to eat room, and the window title, which needs
room to shrink to an ellipsis. Everything else keeps its fill inside
center pills and its set width everywhere else, instead of clock and
media ballooning in turn.

The media-and-resources pairing is the one exception: media asks for
its minimum and takes back the room resources leaves, an exchange
that only means something inside a pill with a set width. That pill
keeps its width floor and media keeps its fill in every section, so
the pair reads the same wherever it sits.

That alone still left the surplus unowned: a row wider than its
content does not push items to its edge — columns with no stretch
share the leftover in proportion to their size, so free-standing
pills drifted apart across the section. The stock arr
commitNotes.76899afe4:
The tray is a BarGroup, whose default property places children in a
GridLayout, and anchoring an item a layout manages is undefined
behavior that also logged a warning on every relayout. Centring
through the layout's own alignment puts the row in the same place
without fighting it.
commitNotes.db4c29ee8:
The time readouts render in the UI font, whose digits each take their
own width, so the pill grew and shrank a few pixels every second as the
digits changed. Tabular figures give every digit the same advance; the
pill now only resizes when a readout gains a digit or a section appears,
which the existing width animation already covers.
commitNotes.98cfbaab2:
Media fills inside its pill so a center pill's spare room goes to the
track title — the pill there has a set width, so the fill is bounded.
Off center the pill is as wide as its group-mates make it: put media
beside the window title or clock and the pill legitimately fills the
section for them, and media's fill then split that surplus too, growing
it past its set width. The fill now applies only in center pills, so
off-center media takes its preferred width and the surplus stays with
the widget the section fill exists for. Shortened resources rides the
same scope, being the other half of the stock pairing.
commitNotes.b3a3e0cd2:
Every anchored bar popup centerd itself using the visible pill's width
but positioned the window, and the pill sits a shadow margin inside the
window's anchored edge — so clock, weather, volume and the rest all
rendered that margin off center toward the right, or downward on the
vertical bar. The offset now subtracts the pill's inset, written as the
same expression the background uses for it, so the two cannot drift
apart again.
commitNotes.d274af5dc:
The popup's position was arithmetic from the stock layout — half the
screen minus half the popup minus the widget width — which pinned it to
the center-left spot the widget used to occupy, however the bar is
arranged now.

The widget hands itself to the popup through a shared Item reference,
set on every path that opens it: click, receive view, and a file
dragged onto it. The popup measures that widget against its bar window
once per open — the loader rebuilds the window each time, so the
measurement is current without binding against the layout — centers
itself under it, and clamps to the screen. Anything short of a clean
measurement leaves the stock position in place, and the measurement can
never take the click down with it: publishing is one assignment, and
the placement runs guarded inside the popup. The vertical bar keeps its
own placement.
commitNotes.facf31326:
A group holding a fill-width widget fills its section when placed off
center, which exists so a window title can shrink to an ellipsis rather
than run past its section. Media is on the fill-width list for a
different reason — leftover room inside its own pill goes to the track
title — and promoting that to section level meant a media group moved
to the left or right side stretched across the whole section. The pill
now fills only for widgets that genuinely want section width; media and
the shortened resources keep their fill inside the pill.
commitNotes.df5e4288e:
Editing a different rule meant cancelling, scrolling back, and opening
again: every card's Edit button went dead while the editor was open,
and the only way out was the Cancel at the very bottom of a long
editor. A close button now sits in the editor's top corner, and Edit
stays live on every rule but the one being edited.

Switching does not repoint the open editor — a used ConfigSwitch has
had its checked: binding broken by the click, so the editor is torn
down and rebuilt for the new rule, the same teardown closing has
always relied on. Unsaved changes are dropped on a switch, exactly as
they are on Cancel. Reorder and delete stay locked while the editor is
open, since moving a rule under an editor keyed to its index would
save over the wrong one.
commitNotes.3af94951c:
The picker listed one row per open window under its raw class and
title, so three browser windows made three entries and a person hunting
for their file manager had to know it answers to org.gnome.Nautilus.
It now lists each open app once, under the name its desktop entry
gives it; a class with no entry is tidied instead — reverse-DNS prefix
dropped, dashes opened into spaces, first letters raised. Selecting one
writes the same anchored class pattern as before.
commitNotes.643157b80:
The switch carries the option's real name, xray, so what it writes can
be looked up against Hyprland's own docs. The tooltip already says what
it does in a sentence.
commitNotes.114e1aed9:
A drive picked on the Local tab vanished from it the moment Mount was
pressed, reappearing only under a separate Mounted tab — which read as
the drive disappearing. Mounted entries now stay put: a Mounted category
on the Local tab for block devices and a Mounted shares category on the
Network tab for network filesystems, each with the same one-click
unmount row the old tab had, and the tab itself is gone. The row moves
to a shared component so both categories draw the entries one way.
commitNotes.9eb844837:
The separator component sizes itself with Layout margins, which only
exist inside a layout. The two dividers flanking the center groups are
anchored children instead, so those margins did nothing and the
top/bottom anchors stretched each line across the bar's full height —
past the rounded background, which the Float corner style insets. They
now center at the same short height the layout margins produce, and the
component carries that height itself so any anchored use gets it.
commitNotes.c2d09742f:
The freedesktop thumbnail name is an md5 of the file URI, and the two
halves disagreed on what that URI looks like: the bulk generator gets
its URI from GIO, which leaves @ & = , : $ + raw in a path, while the
picker encoded them through encodeURIComponent. Any wallpaper with one
of those characters in its name hashed to a thumbnail that was never
written and drew as an empty tile. The picker now puts GLib's raw set
back after encoding, and the magick fallback's own urlencode is held to
the same rule so both generators write one name. Semicolons stay
escaped on every side — GLib escapes them too.

commitNotes.4d7a7486b:
Names what the release added, and corrects how the shell's provenance is
described: the dock is no longer offered as an example of what came from
upstream now that four fifths of it is new, and a theme is described by
what it carries rather than as saved colors — colors being the one thing
upstream is already known for.
commitNotes.193d32686:
The generated notes were commit subjects, which read as a work log rather
than a description of what changed for someone using it. A release can
also carry a name now — 1.2.0 is Let there be RICE — carried through the
manifest as an optional field so unnamed releases show no empty slot.
commitNotes.813f2c88d:
The fork carries a fix confirmed on the affected hardware: title bars
render wrong on NVIDIA whenever blur is on, transparent on one driver
branch and a solid block on another, because the rounded-corner mask
clears and writes the stencil buffer without opening the stencil mask
first. Closed, the clear and the write are silently dropped and the
test that follows reads whatever was left in the buffer.

The fork's branch is based on the commit that builds against the
Hyprland we ship rather than on current upstream, which has already
moved to headers 0.56 does not carry. Merging upstream forward is a
0.57 job, kept on mainstream-next until then.
commitNotes.8f56791f6:
The rebuild scripts try their cached last-good ref first and stop at the
first ref that builds, so a machine that already builds the plugin never
looks at the branch again. That is what keeps a routine Hyprland patch
bump down to seconds, but it also means an upstream fix stays invisible
until Hyprland changes enough to break the cached commit — arriving by
accident, months later, or not at all. Nothing in Repair Install cleared
it either.

Dropping the cached ref makes the next run fall through to the branch.
A serial recorded per machine keeps that to once, so ordinary upgrades
still hit the cache. Machines that predate the marker only record where
they stand, since there is no way to tell whether their ref is behind
and refreshing the fleet on arrival would rebuild everyone for nothing;
a fresh install skips the rebuild too, its baked plugin being current.

Bump _PLUGIN_REFRESH_SERIAL when a fix lands upstream that machines need.
commitNotes.3ec465332:
The notification's Install button runs in the weekly check's detached
waiter, which lives in the user manager's cgroup rather than the login
session's scope — polkit maps that to no session at all, so the
passwordless rule (active local wheel) cannot match and there is no
agent to prompt, and the update was refused every time. The same pkexec
from the Welcome app works because the app is a child of the session.

The button now asks the compositor to spawn the pkexec, making it a
session child with exactly the standing the rule already trusts. The
direct call stays as the fallback for a terminal run, and the refusal
notification stays for whatever remains.
commitNotes.7846abb72:
The legacy NVIDIA editions install the branch-matched 32-bit userspace
(lib32-nvidia-580xx-utils and kin) with the driver itself, and those
packages exist in no online repo — the first-boot keyring switch removes
the baked file repo that carried them. pacman -S resolves every named
target against the sync databases before --needed can skip it, so the
Gaming Mode installer naming the already-installed package aborted the
entire transaction with 'target not found', taking Steam and the rest of
the stack down with it.

The lib32 driver is now added only when it is absent and resolvable:
already installed means nothing to do, resolvable (mainline
lib32-nvidia-utils from multilib) means install it, neither means warn
and carry on so the rest of the gaming stack still lands. A nouveau
system no longer picks up the mainline proprietary 32-bit userspace by
default either — lib32-mesa already covers it.
commitNotes.8f9b5ae48:
Every text field built the menu along with itself, and the menu asks the
field whether there is anything to paste. That question goes to the
clipboard, which is quick to answer when something owns the selection and
has no answer at all when nothing does — the installer on live media being
exactly that case, where a password box is often the first field to exist.

Nothing needs the menu until a right click, so nothing builds it until then.
commitNotes.ffdd7dac5:
The curated bullet called it the shell, which is what we call it among
ourselves and not what anyone reading a changelog calls the thing their
fonts changed on.
commitNotes.593941ebd:
The last commit that built was tried before everything else, so once a
machine had one that still compiled it kept it forever and nothing merged
afterwards ever reached it. It is now the way back rather than the first
choice, tried only if the branch itself will not build.

Nothing recorded which sources a plugin came from, only which Hyprland, so
a run could not tell that it had already built these very sources — the
daily timer recompiled them every night to arrive back where it started.
The stamp carries the commit as a second line, and a stamp written without
one reads as unknown, which is what carries existing installs across.
commitNotes.99d6832fc:
The menu names its icons as Material Symbols, and a desktop action carries
an icon theme name instead. The symbol font drew that name as its own
letters, so Code's actions read COM.VISUALSTUDIO.<>.OSS — <> being the
font's own ligature for the word code.
commitNotes.98db9073e:
A menu belonging to a transparent window was drawn straight onto the
wallpaper, which left the text sitting on whatever happened to be behind
it. Nothing frosts a popup unless the compositor is told to.
commitNotes.1b67db16b:
Every theme keeps its wallpaper as wallpaper.jpg, and the scaled copy the
overview plugin is handed was named after that basename alone. All themes
therefore shared one cache entry, and the freshness check compares only
timestamps, so whichever theme wrote it last was shown behind every other
one. Key the entry by the path it came from and the size it was scaled to.
commitNotes.ec875adb7:
The border gradient rewrote its override file and reloaded the whole
config on every palette change, which is every wallpaper change and so
every step of a slideshow — with both lanes off that was two resets of
keys already absent. It remembers what it last wrote and says nothing
when nothing differs.

The window list was fetched when the page loaded, but it is only read
while the editor is open and opening it fetches a fresh one, so that
first list was always discarded. It also carried two fields no caller
reads.

The theme snapshot asked the schema which profile names ship; it asks
the script that owns the schema instead, as the apply already does.
commitNotes.ca1bf64ef:
That release recorded the setting by commenting its line out, so an
upgraded install has -- border_size = 4 where the field should be. That
read as nothing set, which showed the switch on while the compositor had
no borders, and a theme saved from there turned them back on for good.
A commented field now reads as the off value the old toggle meant by it.

Which profile names ship is also answered here now, rather than by each
caller reading the schema and coming to its own conclusion.
commitNotes.9b204117a:
Editing a rule kept the keys the editor has no widget for, but not the
values it can only half-show: a workspace named rather than numbered
became 1, a rounding became nothing, a size on a tiled window was
dropped. Those are set aside with the rest and written back as they
were.

A second save while the first was still running killed it, and the
killed run's exit read as a failure, which reloaded the file over the
newer list — deleted rules came back. Saves queue instead. A theme
landing under an open editor now closes it, so a save cannot land at an
index into a list that has been replaced.

A custom effect's fields were changed inside the array, which notifies
nothing, so the Save button never noticed the rule had become saveable.

The reset re-armed seven switches; the two border-gradient lanes and
Title Bars were not among them and kept showing the old state.
commitNotes.6b3d1a71a:
A store that could not be understood read as an empty list, so the page
showed no rules and the next save wrote that emptiness over the file —
every rule gone, with nothing said. The reason travels with the result
now; a regenerate refuses rather than publishing nothing, and the page
holds back every write until the file makes sense again.

Effect values were never checked for shape, so a size that was a number
instead of a pair either crashed the writer, leaving the rules
unwritable, or was quietly coerced into something else. And a newline in
a pattern ended the Lua string it sat in, silently killing every rule
after it while the run still reported OK.

The two files are published under one lock, so a reader cannot catch the
store from one write and the generated rules from another. The apply
passes --no-reload, which is the second of the two reloads a theme was
still paying for.
commitNotes.deb7b7cf1:
Two ways it could write a file Hyprland cannot parse, and hyprland.lua
requires general.lua without a pcall, so a broken one takes env, rules,
colors and keybinds down with it.

A value was matched up to the first comma, so a colour written the way
Hyprland also accepts it — rgba(20, 20, 20, 0.5) — was read as rgba(20
and the replacement landed in front of the rest of the line. Quoted
strings are now matched whole.

Adding a setting anchored on the last line that began at the top level
of its block, which is the opening line of a nested table when the block
ends with one; the new line went inside that table and left a stray
comma after its brace. The anchor is now the last line that ends back at
the top level.

The file is also read, changed and written back under a lock, with a
temp name of its own: the settings page is live while a theme applies,
and both edit this file. A shared temp name meant one writer could
rename a file the other was still filling.
commitNotes.38a38e133:
Editing a rule rebuilt it from the editor's own fields, so a rule made by
hand or carried by a theme lost anything this editor has no widget for.
Those keys ride along untouched now.

The preview compiles the pattern with the browser's regex, but Hyprland
matches with RE2 — a pattern one accepts and the other doesn't was
treated as invalid and blocked the save. It only means there is nothing
to preview, and says so.

A colour field stopped following its value after the first typed edit,
and the switches on the decorations page kept their old positions
through a reset: both had lost their bindings to an assignment, and both
are re-armed. Summaries build their text through placeholders so a
translation can move the number, and the write helper nothing called is
gone.
commitNotes.42f28c42b:
A snapshot from before the border and corner keys were split carries the
old bools, and borders off meant no border, no gaps and no resize edge —
not just a zero border size. The schema already spells out what each old
bool drove, so the restore reads that table instead of the two mappings
it knew by name.

A failed snapshot left an empty object behind, which now reads as reset
everything to stock; it leaves no file at all, which an apply skips. The
stock animation profile is loaded through pcall like the chosen one, so
a broken profile can no longer take the input and misc config down with
it, and animationProfile joins the motion group its sibling is in.
commitNotes.7ba676f27:
Both files render values from a theme into Lua the compositor evaluates,
and a theme can arrive by import from anywhere. The window-rule custom
value accepted any brace-wrapped text, so a table constructor could hold
a call instead of a list; it now takes a comma-separated run of literals
and nothing else. Decoration strings went in unescaped, so a value
carrying a quote could close it and continue as an expression; the quote
and the backslash are now escaped on both paths that reach Hyprland, and
the vector pair is coerced to numbers rather than pasted.
commitNotes.0ba6d1ff2:
A theme saved before a setting existed says nothing about it, and the
restore used to leave such keys alone — so applying an older theme kept
whatever the previous theme had put there, and the older theme stopped
looking like its save. The new restore verb fills unnamed keys from the
schema defaults instead: stock is what the machine showed when the theme
was saved. Snapshots from before two keys were renamed still say
borders / roundCorners; a false there now restores as its modern
spelling's zero. The completed set feeds both the file write and the
live keyword push, so the compositor hears the same values the config
got.
commitNotes.c03548021:
A saved theme snapshots the rules store, empty list included — no
rules at save time is part of the look. Applying restores through
the owner script's write verb rather than a copy, so an imported
theme's rules pass the same validation the settings page gets.
Themes saved before rules existed carry no file and leave the live
rules alone.
commitNotes.fdd069756:
Per-app exceptions to the sections above it: pick an open window,
or type a pattern and watch which of the windows open right now it
catches, then choose from curated effects — placement, transparency,
frost, chrome, tearing, idle inhibit — with a custom escape hatch
for the rest. Cards reorder because later rules win.

Last section on the page, so the list grows without pushing other
settings around. The editor is built fresh on every open: a clicked
switch keeps its own state over a binding, and a persistent editor
stops following the draft reset. Saving or cancelling scrolls the
page back to the section, where a new rule's card is.
commitNotes.7f4c5df90:
Rules the shell manages live as JSON and compile whole into
userrules.lua, loaded after rules.lua so a rule made in settings
outranks a shipped one for the same window. One direction only:
nothing parses Lua back, and rules written by hand elsewhere are
never read, shown or touched. The write verb holds every effect to
a schema — a custom effect is a field name plus a literal that must
look like one, so the generated file cannot carry anything else
into the compositor's config.
commitNotes.01ad9606c:
Every window section returns to what a fresh install has, from the same
table the track marks are read from — the reset and the dots on the
sliders cannot disagree about what stock is. Title bars go through their
own service, which owns the flag and the plugin's reload; the border
gradient resets through config.json, where its service is watching.
System look and below are left alone: the cursor and the fonts belong to
the whole desktop, not to its windows.

The reader's assignments moved into a function the reset shares, so what
a key drives is written once.
commitNotes.cc0da30a3:
Every section in the window half of the page says so in its title; the
toggle section at the top is part of that half and now says so too.
commitNotes.e7dee1b99:
The animation set moves out of the main config into named profile files —
expressive is the stock set verbatim, joined by snappy, smooth, bouncy and
minimal. A profile is the whole set at once: curves, speeds and styles are
tuned against each other, so they travel together rather than as fourteen
separate knobs. The name in animations/active picks the file at config
load; a missing or unreadable name falls back to the stock profile, and
the file is read with dofile so a reload always sees what is on disk.

The Decorations page offers the profiles in an Animations section of its
own, greyed with the animations toggle. The picker lists whatever the
profile directory holds: shipped profiles keep their translated names and
their order, everything else is named by its filename — so a profile
someone wrote themselves shows up without the page having to know it
exists.

The choice rides the decoration schema as a namefile key: it reads and
writes the one-word file rather than a Lua field, rea
commitNotes.caeb8653f:
Two modes. The default draws from the palette's primary and tertiary at an
angle and is re-derived whenever the palette moves, so it keeps up with the
wallpaper the way everything else does — a pair of literal colors would be
right once and then wrong after the next wallpaper. The role pair itself is
not offered as a choice: every other combination sits too close together to
read as a gradient at all, so that setting was four ways of picking the same
flat border and one that worked.

The second mode holds the two colors literally and stops tracking the
palette, which is the point of asking for them. They are entered with a
swatch, a hex field and an eyedropper. The eyedropper is the one that
matters: a color worth putting in a border is usually already on the screen
somewhere, and hyprpicker returns whatever is under the cursor.

Either way it is written to the shell's override file, which is required
after the generated palette, so matugen regenerating its own border color
leaves this
commitNotes.70c25ee6e:
The last three the blur block holds. Noise puts grain over the blur, which
is what hides the banding a heavy blur leaves on a gradient. Saturation
decides how much colour it keeps from what is behind. See-through blurs
the desktop rather than the windows stacked underneath.

The first two are sliders; the third is a switch, being a switch.
commitNotes.f5a09782d:
Shadow size, falloff and darkness get a section of their own, greyed
while shadows are off, the same way blur's rows behave.

Shadow falloff is the setting that could not be reached before. It sits
after the offset pair inside the shadow block, and a scan that stopped at
the first closing brace never got that far. It runs 1 to 4, the range the
compositor honors — it clamps anything higher to 4, so a longer track was
selling distinctions that all rendered the same shadow. The shipped
config said 10 and drew 4; it says 4 now.

Size and falloff only shape the shadow; whether any of it shows is the
alpha of its color, and that had no control. A darkness slider carries it.
The hue is kept from whatever the color already is, so a theme that tints
its shadow keeps the tint while the darkness moves. The color travels
through the schema as the whole rgba string, which gives the reader and
writer their first string-typed key: parsing strips the quotes, rendering
restores them and escapes what it
commitNotes.f250d71b5:
Four more settings the compositor has always had, in a Shape section
beside the toggles that switch them on: corner radius, border thickness,
and the gaps between windows and around the screen edge. Each is a row
against the schema.

A slider row can ask for a shorter track. The label had 120px whatever it
said, and anything longer ran underneath the track — "Fullscreen windows"
sat on top of its own slider. Long labels are cut short rather than
allowed to overlap, and the rows that need the room take a 340px track
instead of the rest of the line.

The Borders switch no longer resets the gaps. It set them to 4 and 5 on
its way through, from when there was nowhere else to put them; with rows
of their own that would undo whatever was chosen there. A theme saved
before those rows existed still zeroes them, so an old theme looks the way
it did.

The marker each track carries sits at the start of its own range rather
than at 1, which on a track that stops at 0.8 was drawn past the end.
commitNotes.c6787734f:
Five settings the compositor has always had and the page never offered:
blur radius and passes, the focused and unfocused window
opacities, and how far an unfocused window is dimmed. Each is one row
against the schema — no new parsing, no new restore path, and a theme
saved now carries all of them.

A slider emits on every pixel of a drag, and each write is a process and a
round trip to the compositor, so the changes are collected and sent once
the drag settles. Several sliders moved together arrive as one change.

Blur radius and passes are greyed rather than hidden when blur is off, and
the dim amount likewise when dimming is off: the setting stays where it
was found instead of the page rearranging itself as things are toggled.

The two opacities are not written in the shipped config — Hyprland
defaults them — so their lines appear the first time one is moved.

Both sections go above System look rather than below it. System look picks
the app style, the icon set and the mouse cursor,
commitNotes.53c3b59e1:
The settings page, the snapshot a saved theme takes, and the restore an
apply performs each parsed and rewrote general.lua themselves, in three
languages — regexes in the page's JavaScript, in the snapshot's Python, and
in apply-theme's. Six settings across three implementations was tolerable;
it is the shape that stops being tolerable, because nothing keeps the three
in agreement and a disagreement shows up as a setting that saves but does
not come back.

They share one now. decorations.py knows where each setting lives and
nothing else does; a schema file lists the settings and every site iterates
it. Adding one is a JSON object rather than three regexes.

Where a setting lives is derived from its hyprctl keyword rather than
written down twice: decoration:blur:size is the field `size`, inside
`blur`, inside `decoration`.

Blocks are found by matching braces. The old scan ran to the next `}`,
which cannot reach a field sitting after a nested block has closed —
render_power is behind s
commitNotes.bcea466c7:
A right click on a text field opened the toolkit's editing menu, drawn in
a style nothing else on the desktop uses. The fields draw the same menu
every other right click gets — the shadowed surface card with ripple rows
— offering cut, copy, paste and select all, each row live only when its
action can do something. A field showing dots instead of characters keeps
its content out of the clipboard: cut and copy stay disabled however much
is selected. The toolkit's own menu is switched off, since leaving it in
place would open both.
commitNotes.34d249890:
Two strings on the Display page kept the British spelling while every
other string says color. The translation keys follow the source strings,
so each file carries the new key in the old one's place.
commitNotes.0b783abbf:
A slider's value is bound to the setting it edits and animates towards it, so
a setting changed anywhere else — a theme apply, another window, an edit to
config.json — walks the handle across a run of intermediate values. Saving on
valueChanged wrote one of those back, and once written the binding settled
there: the clock font sliders, with no equality guard at all, came to rest a
fraction below whatever they were aimed at.

moved() is emitted for a drag or a key press and never for a change that came
in through the binding, which is the distinction that was missing. The track
still follows the bound value, so a setting changed elsewhere moves the handle
without being written back.
commitNotes.d4d80ac53:
A window rule blanked blur on every window, so the blur settings reached
only the shell's own surfaces, and a window made translucent showed what
was behind it untouched. The compositor already skips opaque windows —
blur is computed only where alpha falls below one — so windows at full
opacity look and cost exactly what they did, and the transparency
settings are what bring the frost in.

The xwayland menu rule stays: those buffers carry their own shadows, and
blurring them draws a halo around every context menu.

The blur brightness line is gone because one is the value at which both
of its shader branches leave the image untouched.
commitNotes.95862df83:
Two limits in the writer behind HyprlandConfig, both reached by the border
colour and neither by anything using it today.

A key whose last part contains a dot came out as
{general={col.active_border=...}}, which Lua will not parse — a bare name
cannot hold a dot. It is written as a bracket string now. Every caller so
far separates with colons only, so nothing was producing this yet.

Values could only be scalars. A gradient in Lua is a table:
{colors={"rgba(..)","rgba(..)"},angle=45}. The single-string form hyprlang
takes is rejected outright — "invalid color" — so the shell had no way to
express one. --set-lua writes a value through untouched for that case.

The file this writes is required after both the generated palette and the
custom overrides, so what it holds survives a theme apply: with a border
set here, matugen regenerating its own value leaves the override standing,
and resetting the key puts the palette back.

An edit applies itself: the file is replaced atomically, which
commitNotes.8a1dccb6e:
Locks and fallbacks.

The derivatives lock had no timeout, and the section it guards re-encodes
with ImageMagick and can reach pkexec for the login background. Bounded at
thirty seconds; a run that gives up still does its work, so a wallpaper
change costs a derivative that may land out of order rather than a
subshell parked forever.

The Papirus base is checked before anything is published. Only */places is
overridden and the rest is inherited, so with no base on disk the theme
resolves to bare hicolor — every icon on the desktop. Nothing to layer on
now means nothing published and the icon theme left as it was. The
readback also samples an alias beside folder.svg, since the links are laid
down one at a time and a directory holding the newer folder.svg over
aliases from the previous colour otherwise reads as finished.

A restage that is skipped leaves a marker. Waiting is what this script may
never do, but forgetting is not required: a burst now lands the last
palette rather than the f
commitNotes.3205817aa:
config.json. The three places switchwall edits it — the wallpaper path, the
thumbnail path, the accent colour — each read it, filtered it through jq
into a temp named after the file itself, and renamed that over the top,
with no lock. The temp name being fixed is what turns a lost update into a
broken file: two writers open the same path, one renames a document the
other is still writing, and what lands is truncated JSON. An unreadable
config is an empty wallpaper path, which is the invisible bar. They share
one helper now, with a unique temp beside the target and a short bounded
lock; failing to take the lock still writes, since a rewrite that raced is
better than one that never happened.

general.lua. Both writers replaced it in a way that empties it first — one
copying in from /tmp across filesystems, the other opening it for writing
and refilling on close — while switchwall leaves a hyprctl reload running
in the background that can parse it at any moment. A reload landing inside
th

commitNotes.fc489658c: The "Steam Big Picture" step of mainstream-welcome-install always adds lib32-nvidia-utils for any NVIDIA GPU (PCI vendor 10de), regardless of which driver branch is actually installed. On cards that need a legacy branch — e.g. a GTX 1050 (Pascal) running nvidia-580xx-utils — this pulls in mainline nvidia-utils and conflicts with the already-installed legacy driver on nvidia-libgl. Since the transaction runs --noconfirm, pacman can't prompt to resolve it, and the whole step fails.
commitNotes.6b89a4367:
_gpu_nvidia_has_driver passed all seven driver package names to a single
`pacman -Qq`, which exits 1 unless every one is installed. Since the branches
conflict with each other that can never hold, so the probe was always false and
silently skipped the entire NVIDIA path in both orchestrators: no
nvidia_drm.modeset=1 on the kernel cmdline, no /etc/modprobe.d/nvidia.conf, no
deferred KMS, no suspend/hibernate/resume units, and none of the GBM_BACKEND /
LIBVA_DRIVER_NAME / NVD_BACKEND / hypridle tweaks.

Query one package at a time and return on the first hit. The test harness stubbed
the probe out, so the semantics were never exercised; fixture it at the new
pacman seam instead and assert any-of behaviour.
commitNotes.880a9650c:
Limine boots a BIOS machine from stages 1-2 in the MBR and stage 3
(limine-bios.sys) on the boot filesystem, all from one package build. Upgrading
limine replaces stage 3 and cannot touch the MBR, and Arch ships no hook to
reconcile them — so the boot after a routine `pacman -Syu` drops straight into
firmware setup with no bootloader and no error.

Ship limine-bios-sync and 61-limine-bios.hook from mainstream-system, which the
ISO already installs. Package-owned means it reaches machines already in the
field on their next upgrade, not just fresh installs. No-op on UEFI.
commitNotes.dce475292:
The weekly check told the user a new DaVinci Resolve was out and left them to
run the installer themselves. Put the action on the notification instead.

Pressing Install now hands off to `pkexec mainstream-welcome-install
resolve-update` — the same privileged path the Welcome app's install button
already uses, and already covered by 49-mainstream-welcome.rules, so this adds
no new privileged code, no new polkit rule, and no password prompt on a local
session. Nothing runs unless the button is pressed; --no-action removes it.
commitNotes.42584c974:
The Resolve version check was added as a second Component.onCompleted on the
root ApplicationWindow, which already had one for reapplyTheme(). QML allows one
assignment per property per object, so the whole config failed to load:

  Property value set multiple times

Move refreshResolve() into the existing handler. Same behaviour, one handler.
commitNotes.af918239c:
The Updates service shells out to checkupdates, which by construction cannot
see a local package — so the one piece of software Mainstream installs that way
was the one the update UI could say nothing about.

Updates.qml gains the Resolve state, read from `install-davinci-resolve --check
--json` so the version logic stays in one place. refreshResolve() is on demand
only, deliberately not wired to the existing 120-minute checkInterval: one
request to Blackmagic every two hours from every install is the stampede the
timer's RandomizedDelaySec exists to avoid. Every failure path leaves the
properties untouched, so the UI degrades to exactly what it showed before.

welcome-tutorial.qml relabels the two Resolve rows — Install / Installed /
Update to X.Y.Z — and locks a row that is already current so the button cannot
kick off a no-op. Package-to-row matching is prefix-based, so a beta claims its
row without implying a version comparison.
commitNotes.3651449d9:
A thin wrapper around `install-davinci-resolve --check --json` — it owns no
version logic of its own, so the two can never disagree about what "out of
date" means.

It notifies and nothing else: no pkexec, no sudo, no call into
mainstream-welcome-install. The notification names the new version and the
exact command to run; running it is the user's decision.

Each version is announced once, tracked in
$XDG_STATE_HOME/mainstream-resolve/last-notified, since the timer fires weekly
and Blackmagic can go months between releases. --force re-notifies, --quiet
reports through the exit status only.

Exit codes mirror --check (0 / 10 / 1), with one deliberate exception: a failed
check exits 0 in silence. This runs on a timer, and a laptop that wakes on a
train with no network must not produce an error notification.

heading rather than as something being reported. It moves into the same kind of

commitNotes.7294116fa:
The manifest derived everything from commit subjects, so a release could only
ever say what one commit said. The first release had no predecessor tag to diff
against and derived nothing at all.

release-notes.json now overrides summary and changes for named versions only.
Everything else stays derived, so the default cannot drift and every deviation
is visible in one file. Kind stays tag-driven — the tag is the right place to
say how important a release is. A curated list is not capped either: the cap
exists because a derived list is however long the commit range happened to be,
while a curated one is exactly what someone chose to say.

Alongside that, every release carries its unedited range: commits as
"<short sha> <subject>", commitNotes for the commits that wrote a body, merges
when the first-parent walk stepped over any, and commitsTotal when the cap

commitNotes.51b31d0fa:
Sixty-five interface strings landed with the bar layout editor, theme import
and export, the Decorations page, the release indicator and its popup, the
cursor and shake-to-locate settings, and the font picker. None of them existed
in any language file, so none could be translated at all.

All fourteen files gain the same sixty-five keys, each holding the English
text. That is what the extraction tool writes for a new key, and it is what the
rest of these files already look like: between half and three quarters of every
language is still the English placeholder waiting on a translator.

Deliberately not machine-translated. A placeholder announces itself — a
translator can find every outstanding string by looking for a value equal to
its key — while a plausible but wrong translation reads as finished work and
survives review. Getting them right is for people who speak the language.
commitNotes.2bbacaaf1:
The monitor-arrangement canvas sized each rectangle from the mode's
pixel width/height while positioning it from x/y, which hyprctl reports
in logical coordinates. On a scaled display the rectangle came out too
big and its neighbour was pushed too far away — a 4K at 1.666667 was
drawn 3840 wide and shoved the next monitor 3840 across instead of 2304.
Rotation was ignored entirely, so picking Portrait left the preview
rectangle landscape.

Add a logicalSize() helper that swaps the axes for transforms 1/3/5/7
and divides by the scale, matching what Hyprland does, and use it for
the sizes in canvasLayout, resolveEffectivePos and the canvas delegate.
The scale comes from monitors.lua rather than hyprctl's JSON, which
prints it to two decimals and would turn 1.666667 into 1.67 — a 5px
error per monitor that accumulates across the row.

Preview only: the applied configuration was already correct, because

commitNotes.003aabe9e:
The switch to a Lua greeter config only reached fresh installs. exp-update,
which is what updatems runs, never re-runs the setups step, so a machine
installed before the switch kept its .conf and kept showing the deprecation
notice at every login with nothing to clear it.

updatems-system already refreshes the greeter's neighbours — the background
helper and both polkit files — on every update, and runs as root, so the
migration goes there. It only acts when the greeter directory already exists,
so it will not set one up on a machine that never asked for one.

Hyprland looks for hyprland.lua before hyprland.conf, so writing the new file
is what actually resolves it. The old one is moved to hyprland.conf.old rather
than deleted, and only once the write has succeeded: if a greeter somehow will
not start, renaming one file puts it back. That is the same thing the installer
already does with a user's own pre-Lua config.

The config itself moves out of the heredoc into sdata/sddm/hyprland.l
commitNotes.75e85438a:
The ISO writes this config from post-install-login; ./setup writes the same one
from here, so both had to move together or a scripted install would still show
the .conf deprecation notice on the login screen.

Byte-identical to the archiso copy. The old .conf is removed first, so a machine
installed before this stops carrying both.
commitNotes.45d340364:
The guard reads two stamps: /var/lib/hyprland-plugins/hyprland-version for the
Hyprland this system has, and <plugin>.builtfor for the one each .so was built
against. It returned true whenever either was missing, and nothing but the
rebuild scripts ever wrote them. Those run from the pacman hook on a hyprland
upgrade, or from a timer five minutes after boot -- neither has happened yet the
first time a new install reaches the greeter. So every fresh install loaded both
plugins with no version check at all, which is the one moment a mismatched .so
is most likely, and a segfault at dlopen there is a login loop.

The system version now gates the check. Absent, this is not an install whose
plugins we manage and the check still passes open. Present, a .so with no stamp
is refused rather than trusted -- the same conclusion quarantine_stale_targets
already reaches when it moves a stampless plugin aside.

./setup now writes both halves: the system version before it builds, so a failed
build sti
commitNotes.dd6b20bf6:
The guard records which Hyprland a plugin was built against, and it read that
from pkg-config, which reports 0.56.1 and knows nothing about the package
release. A rebuild that only moves the release changes the ABI: 0.56.1-1 to
0.56.1-2 landed today, rebuilding Hyprland against aquamarine 0.14.0, which
flips _aq_0.13 to _aq_0.14 inside the hash a plugin checks at load. The stamp
either side of that read 0.56.1, so the guard would have compared them equal and
handed back a plugin built against the older ABI.

It asks pacman first, which reports 0.56.1-2, and keeps pkg-config as the
fallback so a rebuild against a hand-built Hyprland still works.

All four scripts move together. The version they write is read back by
quarantine_stale_targets, by each .so's .builtfor file, and by the check in
custom/general.lua that runs at every login — change one and the comparison
fails closed, silently disabling both plugins.
commitNotes.8dfc1fdd6:
Settings swaps one Loader's source to navigate, so the Themes page is torn
down and rebuilt every time it is opened — and again on every apply, since
a theme change bumps Appearance.themeRevision and forces a page reload. Each
rebuild re-read and re-decoded every preview.png, which are full-monitor grim
screenshots: 24 MB and about 450ms of decode across five saved themes, scaling
linearly with the number of themes.

Three things had to change together, because any one alone leaves the reload
visible:

The index, last-applied slug and their loader processes move to a new
ThemeLibrary singleton, so a rebuilt page has its grid populated on the first
frame instead of after two subprocesses return. That removes the empty-grid
phase and the "— None —" flash in the Day/Night dropdowns.

The previews drop cache: false. The ?v=<created> token already in their URLs
is the invalidation mechanism and is restamped at millisecond resolution
everywhere preview.png is written, so a replaced screensho
commitNotes.b94b321c5:
Opening an app made the whole dock slide sideways for a moment and settle back.
It was never the click: the app list is a binding over the open windows, so a
window appearing re-ran it and handed the model a brand new object for every
app, including all the ones that had not changed. The model treated each as a
new item, the dock dropped and re-added every icon, its appearance transition
ran, and the animated width moved the centred row.

That also explains why it only happened on a launch. Dragging re-runs the same
binding but suppresses the transition while reordering, and clicking an app that
is already open or right-clicking it never touches the window list at all.

Entries are now kept between runs and updated in place, so unchanged apps keep
their identity and their delegates. An app that genuinely appears or goes away
still gets a new or destroyed entry and still animates.

Worth having on its own: every open window used to rebind every dock delegate.
commitNotes.049964f57:
Cherry-picked from upstream, with the launch animation defaulting to Bounce.

Three places needed a decision rather than a straight merge:

Upstream played the animation on every click. Here a click also opens an app
folder or toggles a window preview, and neither is a launch — animating those
would say something happened that did not. It now plays only in the branch that
actually starts the app.

The icon loader keeps its exclusion of folders, which have their own loader and
never launch, and gains the animation transform.

The tint overlay had to repeat that transform. It is anchored to fill the icon,
but anchors follow geometry and scale/rotation do not touch geometry — so with
Tint app icons on, the tint would have sat still while the icon moved under it.

The picker sits under Tint app icons in Interface settings, where the rest of
the dock's appearance options are.
commitNotes.251af81da:
Slotting the release indicator into layouts saved before it existed meant
recording which ids had been offered, and recording that meant writing the
config file from the load handler. At 1.0.5 that handler was one line and the
shell wrote this file exactly once, when it created it — nothing else touched it
at startup.

That is a property worth having back. A first login sets the wallpaper path from
outside the shell a moment after login, and it works only because nothing else
writes the file afterwards. Adding a startup write puts a second writer into
that window for the sake of one widget appearing on its own.

So the seeding goes, and with it the record it needed. Someone upgrading will
not find the release indicator in their bar; it is in the layout editor with
everything else. A widget you have to add yourself is a smaller cost than a
first boot that comes up unthemed.

The legacy-switch migration stays: it only fires for a file written before
bar.layout existed, which no fresh ins
commitNotes.cee970e26:
Llano/Sumo, Wrestler and Trinity/Richland sit well above the pre-GCN id
ceiling and advertise HD 7xxx/8xxx names, so neither the id test nor the
name regex saw them. They were handed the amdgpu-only autoconfig arm
despite needing the radeon module, and a RADV package set that has no
support below GCN1.

Match their four id windows exactly, so the GCN APUs sharing those pages
stay modern: Kabini/Temash, Mullins, Carrizo/Stoney and Kaveri.
commitNotes.963589125:
RADV is GCN1+ only, so vulkan-radeon enumerates zero devices on pre-GCN
parts, and because it provides 'vulkan-driver' it also satisfied the
catch-all and suppressed the lavapipe fallback, leaving no working Vulkan
at all. Install mesa alone there and let the catch-all supply swrast.

VA-API is part of mesa itself now, so the retired libva-mesa-driver
target goes with it. Aligns ./setup and the gpu-drivers tool with the
ISO install.
commitNotes.d9c41c47f:
Intel package selection carried no generation signal, so every Intel GPU
received one flat set: the iHD VA-API driver alongside the legacy i965
driver, and never an OpenCL runtime.

Add INTEL_GEN (xe|modern|legacy|none) to gpu_detect. Intel device ids are
not monotonic, so the tiers match known id prefixes newest-first with a
name fallback for Arc/Iris Xe; anything unrecognised falls to 'modern',
which is safe on any Gen8+ part.

The tiers track the two boundaries that actually change packages:
  xe      Gen12+/Arc — the only tier upstream's compute runtime and the VPL
          runtime support; gets intel-compute-runtime + ocl-icd + vpl-gpu-rt
  modern  Gen8-Gen11 — iHD VA-API, no OpenCL. Upstream moved Gen8-11 compute
          to legacy1 packages that Arch does not ship, so the runtime would
          be ~346 MB that cannot enumerate a device
  legacy  Gen4-Gen7.5 — i965 VA-API, the driver that actually covers this
          hardware; predates iHD entirely

commitNotes.4a80440ca:
Four changes, drawn from two community installers and checked against this
machine rather than taken on trust.

A launcher wrapper replaces the bare symlink, and the desktop entry now routes
through it, so a menu launch gets the same treatment as a terminal one. It
unsets QT_QPA_PLATFORMTHEME and QT_STYLE_OVERRIDE, which the session sets to
qt6ct while Resolve's bundled Qt 5.15 ships no platformthemes plugins at all,
and on a hybrid laptop it exports the PRIME offload variables. Without those,
the GL context comes from the iGPU while OpenCL runs on the NVIDIA card, and
clCreateContext fails across the split — Resolve hangs on the Color page. The
detection runs at launch, not at install, so a MUX flip or a dock is picked up,
and every gate is required: opencl-nvidia depends only on zlib, so an NVIDIA
box can have no GLX vendor library, where exporting the vendor name turns a
working launch into a GLX failure. Two lspci calls, because lspci honours only
the last -d and one call would hav
commitNotes.2967d5ff3:
The dock's preview tiles bound a ScreencopyView straight at the toplevel
with no gate, so both close paths tore the window down underneath a live
capture. hidePreview() only starts a fade — the Loader stays active and
the capture stays attached — so the toplevel died while the tile was
still capturing it, and Wayland answers that with a fatal EINVAL
protocol error that takes the whole shell with it.

Latch the capture off before dispatching the close on both the
middle-click and the close-button path. The latch is one-way for the
life of the tile: nothing here tells a client refusing to close apart
from a close still in flight, and the next preview builds the tile
fresh. Same guard the overview carries.
commitNotes.8af023054:
The closing latch that quiesces a window preview before dispatching a
close never cleared, so a client that refuses to quit — an unsaved-changes
prompt is the usual reason — left its tile inert for the rest of the
overview session: no hover, no click, no tooltip, and a stuck hover tint.

Split the latch. `closing` now drives only the input gates and clears
itself after a one-second grace period, while a new monotonic
`captureSuppressed` drives captureSource. Nothing here can tell a refused
close apart from one still in flight, so the capture stays down until the
next overview open rebuilds the tile; re-attaching to a toplevel that then
dies is the fatal Wayland error this guards against.
commitNotes.31fc57c07:
About names the release next to the brand, and the System Update header
carries the transition the button is about to perform, so the version is
visible both where you look up what you are running and where you decide
whether to update. The arrow only appears while a release is actually
waiting; otherwise the header shows the installed version alone.

ContentSection gains titleExtra alongside headerExtra. The version belongs
against the title it qualifies, and headerExtra sits the other side of the
spacer that pushes buttons to the far end of the row, so it could only ever
render against the Copy button.

Reading these values instantiates ReleaseUpdates in the settings process as
well as the shell, so announcements are now gated behind _announceEnabled,
which only the shell sets. Without that, opening Settings could raise a
second notification for a release already announced. This mirrors how
ThemeManager keeps its Day/Night scheduler to the main shell.
commitNotes.85e4637cf:
Arch builds gnome-software without the PackageKit plugin — its shipped plugin
set has flatpak, fwupd, appstream, even dpkg, and no packagekit at all, and
packagekit is not among its optional dependencies. So the store has never
handled native packages here and cannot be configured into doing so; the
plugin is a compile-time option, not a setting.

The description said otherwise, and every person installing Mainstream read it
in the Included Extras list. The PKGBUILD's optdepends is generated from this
same file, so it corrects itself on the next build.
commitNotes.a464a7151:
The bootstrap cloned the mainstream branch and left the clone on its tip,
so a script install landed ahead of every numbered release with no record
of which release it descended from. Two things followed from that missing
marker: the desktop's release indicator read the install as unversioned
and stayed silent, and the next updatems run reset the clone to the newest
tag rather than seeing it was already past it.

Resolve the newest release tag with the same pattern updatems matches,
check the branch out at it, and write .updatems-applied-tag once setup
succeeds. --edge keeps the previous behaviour and marks itself with the
release it descends from, so an edge install still reports a version and
updatems leaves it alone until a release reaches it.

Both channels land on a branch rather than a detached HEAD, since setup's
branch detection tries to bounce a detached HEAD back to main or master
and neither exists in this clone.
commitNotes.a445163e4:
The arrangement the bar ships with was written out twice — once as the
config defaults a first run gets, once inside the settings page for its
"Reset to defaults" button. Nothing held the two together, so adding a
widget meant remembering to edit both, and forgetting would have given
Reset a different bar than a fresh install.

Declare it on Config and have the adapter and the settings page read the
same thing.
commitNotes.7ceb2fc70:
The generator explained itself in terms of what the desktop does with the
result — which dot colour a kind produces, and a per-kind notification
filter that no longer exists. Say what the field is instead and leave the
presentation to the thing presenting it.

The schema number went out with every manifest and nothing has ever read
it. A version nobody checks is worse than none: it suggests a bump would be
handled somewhere.
commitNotes.21c254948:
A popup that only shows while the pointer is over its widget closes when
the pointer leaves, and has nothing to say to the focus grab. It was still
listening for a dismissal it could never act on, and unregistering itself
on teardown from a list it was never added to — so every bar widget you
hovered over built a connection to the grab and emitted a signal into
nothing. Only the click-triggered popups take part now.
commitNotes.903e9315d:
The manifest copy and the record of which release has already been
announced were written into the dotfiles clone, next to the tag file
updatems owns. They are untracked there, and updatems stashes untracked
files and hard-resets that tree on every run — and re-clones it outright
when the branch has moved on. So the record of what the user had already
been told was thrown away by the very thing that made a new release worth
telling them about, and the notification came again for a release they had
already seen.

Put the cache under the cache directory and the record under state, where
the rest of the shell's own files live. Only the applied tag stays in the
clone, because updatems writes that one.
